utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Mr. Prstojevic, the document on the basis of which municipal War Presidencies in general were established. Have you ever seen that document?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, but I believe war commissions are a totally different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you've answered the question. You've never seen such a document. We are close to the end of the tape. Anyhow, Mr. Tieger, would there be any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we are to adjourn because we are running out of tape. Would it be possible to prepare for the protective measures because I do understand that it takes 20 minutes. I'm afraid we would need then another break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All preparations can be made. The one problem is that there kind of a protection for this witness. Do the parties agree that we could for the few questions where all of it was in all respects public - that means that all the public could also see the back of the head of this witness - that we would continue with this shield already in place?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm simply not understanding what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue is for the next witness we need the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we would need another break to put that there. Would there be any objection if the last few questions to this witness would be put to him where the public could not see the back of his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If that's the only change, Your Honour, then I -- it doesn't seem sensible to have any objection if Mr. Prstojevic doesn't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A simple no would have done. Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was being cooperative and helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're running out of tape, Mr. Stewart. We'll adjourn until 25 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps the documents that were presented to the witness by Mr. Krajisnik could be briefly placed before him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please assist Mr. Tieger. Did you have one of them specifically in mind, Mr. Tieger? Re-examined by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I want to direct your attention and the Court's attention to the document at the back of the materials. The instructions of December 19th were identified as number 1. And as number 2 there are diary -- handwritten diary entries that you also had a brief opportunity to look at. The accused began his questions by asking you to confirm that you were unsure about the precise date of the meeting at which the instructions were distributed or of the precise nature of that meeting, and I believe you did. Looking at the -- and then subsequent to that he asked you to draw a conclusion from the -- from one of the diary entries that the document was distributed at the session of the Serbian Assembly. Looking now at item number 2, the handwritten diary entries, do you see that it reflects --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My headphones don't seem to be working. I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher. Can you now hear, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll begin again then, sir. I was asking you to direct your attention to the documents at the back of the materials, that is the documents that were marked as 1 and 2, 1 being the instructions of December 19th and 2 being the handwritten diary entries that you had a brief opportunity to look at. Now, the accused began his questions to you about those documents by asking you to confirm that you were unsure about the precise date of the meeting at which the instructions were distributed or of the precise nature of that meeting. He then asked you to look at a diary entry and asked you to draw a conclusion that the instructions were distributed at the session of the Serbian Assembly. I'd like you now to look at number 2, the handwritten diary entries. And is it correct that on the first page of number 2 we see a meeting of the Main Board and the deputies' club on December 20th, 1991? And then on the second page there is a reference to the Serbian Assembly in the Holiday Inn on Saturday, which would be December 21st. Do you see both of those entries? The second entry would be the -- or the second entry to which I referred should be reflected in the second-to-last entry on the page.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. I see it, but in this document it's the way we said when Mr. Krajisnik was asking questions, because it's obvious that other meetings took place before the Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not the December 19th instructions were distributed to some people at those earlier meetings? And if you don't know, just tell us that.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think that they were distributed only at that meeting, at the Assembly session, because I never heard about those instructions before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik also directed your attention to a document that was marked number 4. Now, if I could ask you to look at that quickly. Now, this is a document establishing the Serbian Assembly of Ilidza on the 3rd of January, 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the heading indicates, that decision was taken pursuant to the instructions of December 19th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a copy of that decision was sent to, among others, President Krajisnik, is that right, as you see on the second page?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is exactly the copy that we see here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked on Thursday at page 71 whether or not the appointment -- your appointment to the position of secretary of inspections was a local decision. Is it correct, Mr. Prstojevic, that you believed you were to receive the position of secretary for the economy but that an intervention took place from either Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Karadzic and another person was appointed to secretary of the economy and you received the position of secretary of the inspections?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but I think this time we're talking about an intervention by Mr. Karadzic because a man came, I can't remember his last name at the moment. It's a certain neki Bozo [as interpreted]. He became the secretary for the economy and then I was given or I took up this other post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood from your earlier interview that you were not sure whether it was Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Karadzic. What makes you think at this point that this intervention was by Mr. Karadzic rather than by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how the intervention would have been made. I know that the brother of this man, Bozo, whose last name I cannot remember -- because later in the war he was the president of the Chamber of Commerce of Republika Srpska. The brother was very close, allegedly, to President Karadzic. So I really don't know how it went. But that's why I think that the intervention came from Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this morning you were -- there was a brief reference to Mr. Ceklic who became secretary of the Crisis Staff in April, I believe you indicated, after previously being secretary of the Assembly I think you said.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Momo Ceklic is the secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Ilidza since the formation of the multi-party Assembly following the elections in November 1990. As of April, 4th of April, 1992, the Crisis Staff would be carrying out the functions which were supposed to be implemented by the Assembly but it could not meet. So then the secretary would be the -- secretary would also be a member of the Crisis Staff and would be participating in its work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Ceklic someone who was close to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ceklic knew Mr. Krajisnik much better. I think that they also went to school together at some point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. -- was Mr. Ceklic someone through whom information could be conveyed about what Ilidza was doing and what Ilidza should do from republican leaders, generally, and more specifically from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary of the Municipal Assembly is a very important person, and he's responsible for the administrative correspondence. So all the consultations, interventions could be done that way and it was normal for him to be working together with the secretary of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and other officials, according to the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't asking about Mr. Ceklic's work as the secretary of the Municipal Assembly with respect to his activities in connection with the operation of the joint government. I simply wanted to know whether Mr. Ceklic's personal relationship with Mr. Krajisnik facilitated the flow of information from the republic leadership to Ilidza and back. And by that, I mean the republic leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he did facilitate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing further, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't -- no, it's all right. I'll leave that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need for further questions triggered by the questions put to the witness in re-direct? If there's not, the Chamber has no questions for the witness. Mr. Prstojevic, this means that this concludes your evidence. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague to testify, to answer all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will not deal with all of the exhibits because we will first have to identify to what extent the exhibits presented by Mr. Krajisnik are already in evidence, some of them certainly are, and to see whether translations are there. So we'll work on that and not at this moment give a decision. However, there's another matter. That's the context of the interview. I noted that pages 11, 12, and 13 might be needed to create the appropriate context, and that is then from the large interview, that's the 207-page interview. I also noted pages 40 and 41. And the last issue, Mr. Tieger, where you were asking attention for the context and you were asking that the witness would not be misled was, from what I understand, page 48 of the interview. So just to create a sufficient context, I would suggest that pages 47, 48, and 49 would be in evidence. I don't know who's going to tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think it matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just ask for the opportunity to briefly -- since we're -- since some of the exhibit issues are pending anyway, I'd just like for the opportunity to look that over quickly and some of the other contextual issues that have arisen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we'll finally deal with the exhibit numbering. We'll do that at another moment. Is there any other procedural issue related to witness this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One, Your Honour. I know the Court had discussed with the witness the possibility of seeking his diary. I just wanted to bring that back to the Court's attention since it seems to have been left pending and I don't know whether the Court is considering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We said we are considering it. It has not given -- at least not -- it has not been given any follow-up with the parties, so sometimes the Chamber is active but sometimes also waits. But if the parties would consider it would be useful to have these -- this note -- this personal note, this diary, in evidence or at least to have a look at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it, so to see whether it has any relevance, of course the problem is that we'll not be in a position to ask any additional questions to the witness because it wasn't there, it wasn't translated. So that -- the one step might trigger another one. But I'd just like to know from the parties whether they would like the Chamber to ask the witness to provide it. Both of you uni sono.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well -- yes, I think that would be useful, Your Honour, or potentially useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So does the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then -- we'll then consider that and see whether we can follow your suggestion and whether we'll invite the witness to provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Might I just ask in relation to these vexed interview transcripts. Is the -- I might have to go back and look at the transcripts over the last few days as well. My understanding was that they -- all those transcripts were in evidence in the sense that they -- that they were evidence, that that was what the witness has said when he was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the parties were invited to point the specific portions, so as to create the background for some of the questions. But the parties are free, if you say they need other portions -- if both parties say, We would like to have them in evidence for this purpose, the whole of this, then of course the Chamber would consider it. We have a lot of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I reserve my position and go and review the transcript and come back to it if and as necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If until now the pages I mentioned when the context was specifically raised during the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm not -- I'm not trying to divine the underlying purpose of Mr. Stewart's comment, but I think the Prosecution has made clear its position that once such information of any sort from any source is in evidence, then the Court can use that information as part of the totality of evidence which it relies on to form conclusions about the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's especially the reason why the Chamber would perhaps prefer to have those parts of the interviews available where there's any contextual issue but not be -- well, to say it frankly, not be bothered by information that, at least as far as the substance is concerned, is not in evidence. The parties have an opportunity to further express their views on this. It's clear, Mr. Tieger, you say it's fine if it's all in evidence, but then it's in evidence also to the substance. Mr. Stewart, you would like to consider it. We'll hear from you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd just like to do that, Your Honour. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't imagine that the Defence would not support just admitting it all in evidence on substance as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It seemed to contradict some things that have already been said, Your Honour. It's better if I go away, read the transcript, think about it, which is always a good idea, before I say anything more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Fine. Then are we ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be yielding the table to Mr. Harmon at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need to check the microphones, so we'll have a break of five minutes. If everyone stands by, we'll return once the exercise has been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I'm yielding the table to myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. --- Break taken at 11.54 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I understand that you'll examine Witness KRAJ 068. Protective measures in place, pseudonym, face, and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom. I take it that you'll start with the pseudonym sheet as first exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and just a consideration, Your Honour. If we are in closed session, is there actually a requirement for me to read the 89(F) summary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we are not in closed session. We are in -- the curtains will be pulled up once the witness is there. No one will see his voice, no one will hear his voice, and no one will know his name, but it's still public -- public session, apart from all these limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first document, I take it, will be the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, that would be number -- give it already a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, the pseudonym sheet would be P806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness 068, because that's how we will call you, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness 068, protective measures are in place -- please be seated. The protective measures that are in place is that no one will see your face, it will be distorted on the screens; no one will hear your own voice; and we'll not call you by name. But the evidence you give will otherwise be available for the outside world. Ms. Edgerton, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Edgerton:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 68. Madam Usher has put before you a sheet of paper and I'd like you to have a look at that sheet of paper and tell us if the name and date of birth that appear thereon are yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P806 will be admitted under seal. May I remind counsel that they should switch off their microphones as soon as the witness answers the question and I'll try to not forget it myself as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours with respect to Witness 68, we'll be proceeding under Rule 89(F) and in that regard we've prepared for you a package of, in fact, four separate documents, each one of course would have to receive its own exhibit number. The witness has previously given three statements, one to Bosnian authorities in 1994; one to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995; and a second one in 1996. There's a further document included in that package, and that's a single sheet setting out corrections which the witness has made to the chronology of events as detailed in those previous statements and which he signed and dated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, the first ICTY witness statement of 1995 would be P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, will be P807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the second ICTY signed statement, 20th of May, 1996, I take it would be P808.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Bosnian statement numbered and redacted the 10th of October, 1994, would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P809, and then the corrections signed yesterday would be...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P810, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could please have copies of those four documents put before Witness 68.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, with respect to the statements which are being put before you, I'd like to ask you: Have you had an opportunity to review those statements during the course of your preparation for testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at those statements and tell me if you recognise the signature that appears on them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, subject to the corrections which you'll also be bringing to the attention of the Trial Chamber, do you find these three statements to be correct and do you adopt their contents as correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, they are correct. They are quite correct and I accept them as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the corrections which were drafted yesterday and you signed and dated, was that document read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, it was read out to me in my language and I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've also had an opportunity, I understand, to read a translation of that document in your own language this morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I see on your list, and that's P807, is dated the 21st of October, 1995, I take it should be the 21st and 22nd, because otherwise the next date would be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, there's some paragraphs of Witness 68's 1995 statement don't fall strictly within the parameters of 89(F), those being paragraphs 2, 8, and 9. I'll be leading that evidence live, and that's how I would propose to begin at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 68, could you tell us whether in the year leading up to the war you had occasion to see any high-level SDS leaders in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we getting the -- normally what we do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Get the 89(F) summary before so the public can understand what the evidence is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I see your hand raising to your head. That's -- you may have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's been a while since I've appeared before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I'll read the witness's 89(F) summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is aware of this procedure. Witness, usually those parts of your statement that are on paper and will not be dealt with in open court will be read in the summaries, so the public knows what your testimony is about and what you have stated before. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. "The witness is Muslim from Foca municipality. He's a teacher by training. "The military on attack Foca started on April 8th, 1992. The next day infantry attacked the town, people in JNA uniforms, locals, Montenegrins who wore Chetnik uniforms. The part of Foca where the witness lived was attacked and shelled on April 9th, 1992. He hid in the cellar of his house with his family and others. The attack lasted on and off for three days. "On the second day of the attack" -- pardon me. On April 11 or 12, 1992, the witness was visited by a Serb neighbour who told him that Foca had fallen and he could no longer guarantee the safety of the witness and the witness's family. This neighbour said he had contacts with local commanders and could provide them with an escape route to Montenegro. On that day, the witness and his family, together with a neighbour and his family, left Foca. They were accompanied by their Serb neighbour through a series of checkpoints, all the way to Montenegro. They eventually made their way to Bar, where they registered with the Red Cross and the police. They moved from place to place to avoid harassment and provocation until 21 May 1992, when the witness was arrested by Montenegrin policemen. There were over 20 other Muslims arrested that day altogether. On the first day of his detention in Bar, the witness saw two men from Foca in the police building where he was held. One of these two was a policeman, the other a restaurant owner. The witness met up with this restaurant owner in 1994, and this man at that time told the witness he was sorry he had had him arrested in 1992, but that he had been compelled to. He didn't tell the witness who his superior was. After three days in Bar, the witness and six other Muslim males were transferred to a prison in Herceg-Novi. On 25th May, 1992, additional Muslims from locations in Bosnia were brought to the police station in Herceg-Novi. On 25th May, they were all taken by bus to KP Dom Foca. On their arrival, they were beaten and searched by Serbs, who the witness names. The day after the witness's arrest, he secretly watched out of the windows and counted prisoners on the way to the dining room at KP Dom. There were 567. The warden of KP Dom Foca was Milorad Krnojelac. The witness knew Krnojelac from before the war. During his detention, the witness saw Krnojelac ordering and supervising guards. The witness names the guard commanders and other prison officials, such as the deputy warden, the head of security, inspectors, and guards. During his confinement, the witness was beaten and locked in solitary confinement on four separate occasions, all in 1992. The witness talks about the conditions in solitary confinement as well as in the prison generally, including how little food the prisoners received and how there was no heating. Only those who were very seriously ill received some medical care. While the witness was not interrogated during his detention, 70 per cent of the prisoners in his room were. Until the end of July [sic] 1992, it was a pattern after breakfast until 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon. Men would return from the interrogations badly beaten. The witness was never tried during his incarceration, nor was he ever sentenced. In late June or early July 1992, the witness saw a succession of 36 men killed in four groups. He knew them all. They were non-Serbs from the Foca area. They were taken to the administration building at KP Dom Foca and one by one chained and then beaten to death. After the beating, the prisoners were unchained and their bodies thrown on a blanket, wrapped up, and dragged out. The witness heard nine shots coming from outside the prison after each separate incident and a sound as if trucks were being unloaded. This same scenario repeated itself three more times in exactly the same way with intervals of a couple of days between the second and third groups. The witness recognised the prison guards who took part in the killings, all Serbs. Some time after the incidents, the witness was called out by a guard and he was ordered to clean the room where people had been beaten to death. The floor of the room had blood on it. The practice of taking people away at night lasted until the end of July 1992. From then on, people were taken in small groups to be "exchanged" but were never seen again. The witness notice that 168 detainees disappeared this way. The witness was exchanged from KP Dom on October 6th, 1994, at the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo bridge in Sarajevo. And that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. You may continue to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness 68, to repeat the question I had asked initially a little to hastily, could you tell us whether in the year before the outbreak of war you ever saw any high-level SDS leaders in Foca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I saw Velibor Ostojic and Vojislav Maksimovic and they were SDS functionaries from the republican level. As for the local SDS members, I would see them all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to focus for now on the two people who you've named who were active at the republican level you say, Maksimovic and Ostojic. Could you tell us how you were able to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I knew Maksimovic in person because he had been a friend of my father's for a long time. As for Ostojic, I knew him from the TV and I had occasion to meet him at a business meeting at a hotel. I saw him for the second time in the same hotel that he stayed in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What hotel was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: It was the Zelengora Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that hotel located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: In the Mosa Pijada Street next to the bridge over the Cehotina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Foca, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, drawing you to the year before the war, when you saw these two republican-level officials who you've referred to, where was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I saw them in the immediate vicinity of the premises where I worked. They arrived in a car and went to Miso Petkovic's flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Miso Petkovic a Muslim or -- is Miso Petkovic a Muslim or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Miso Petkovic is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw both these individuals enter Miso Petkovic's flat. Could you tell us approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: It was sometime in 1991, either November or December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them with any other local personalities on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes. With them was Petko Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to both Petkovic and Ivanovic, do you have any knowledge of whether or not they were politically active at the local level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I assume that they were because at all the SDS meetings and organisations they appeared there as good organisers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your statement that at the SDS meetings these men appeared there, is that based on your having seen them at these meetings or having heard some information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I heard information about that and this meeting at the apartment of Miso Petkovic affirmed to me that they were involved in the work of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, apart from having seen them enter this private home, did you see these two republican-level officials in Foca at any other locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them in the fish restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately -- did you see them on only one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: On more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over what period of time was this, do you recall? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: It was the prewar period. This could have been in January or February. I saw them on several occasions in that period, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The times you saw them at this restaurant, do you recall whether or not they were in the company of any local personalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, Miro Stanic was with them, Petko Cancar, Petko Ivanovic, Miso Petkovic, and others that I knew a little less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Miro Stanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Miro Stanic was the president of the SDS in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was Petko Cancar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Petko Cancar succeeded him and he was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can take you to the time of -- if I can jump a little bit forward in time and take you to the time of the attack on Foca and the second day of the attack. Could you tell us where you were that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: On the second day of the attack, there was a truce. A neighbour came to see me from the second floor and he invited me for coffee, me and my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "truce" what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: The shooting stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time this neighbour came to see you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I was on the first floor in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: (redacted). When we went inside the hall, you could hear the buzz of the radio station and then you could hear a voice which said: "Shoot at everything that moves and slaughter everything that comes under your hands."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise that voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised the voice of Mr. Velibor Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On hearing that voice, did you ask your neighbour who it was that was talking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him -- of course my neighbour felt uncomfortable because I heard that. He told me, Listen to that fool, because I said, Was that Ostojic's voice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I take it you understand why a redaction was needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've been told, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After hearing what this voice had said, what then did you think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I don't know -- what do you mean, What did I think? I knew the voice, it was a threatening voice, and I knew that I couldn't stay there any more, I couldn't survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meaning you felt you couldn't stay -- live in your town any longer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you also have occasion to receive any other information about Ostojic's role relating to the takeover of Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I received information from my friend who was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what he told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: He told me directly, All orders and the commands that were being issued in the town were under the auspices of Maksimovic and the Pale leadership and Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, leaving that area of testimony, Witness 68, we can move back to the statements that you gave previously, which have been marked as exhibits, and I'm just going to ask you some additional or clarifying questions with respect to some paragraphs of those statements. First, with respect to your statement given in 1995, paragraph 10, you describe the assistance of a Serb neighbour, which allowed you to escape to Montenegro. Do you think you could have gotten out of Foca on your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No, there was no chance of me doing it by myself, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Because my town had already fallen and the neighbourhood where I lived was encircled or surrounded by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to paragraph 14 of that same statement, you say you saw one Milorad Stevanovic and Zdravko Matovic, both from Foca, on the first day of your detention at the police station. Can I ask you, in the period leading up to the war did you ever see either of these two men Stevanovic or Matovic meeting with high-level SDS leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I'd had the opportunity to see Stevanovic at his establishment. High-ranking officials frequented his establishment. And Matovic I would encounter, of course. He was working as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Ostojic or Maksimovic meeting with Stevanovic in the period leading up to the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, at this establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on one occasion or more than one occasion, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I think it was on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on in your statement from 1995 to paragraph 25. That talks about the bus ride in which you were taken to KP Dom Foca. And I'd like to ask you: Was there anybody else on the bus in addition to the Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: There were another 25 Serbs from Bosnia who had been arrested in Montenegro and were being returned to Republika Srpska, to Bosnia actually, to Foca, to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who drove the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: A Serb driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that driver uniformed or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you under any guard on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: There were two police officers until the border with Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once over the border, were you still under any guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No, only the driver was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, dealing with your arrival at KP Dom Foca, paragraph number 2 -- I misquoted the previous paragraph, by the way. That was paragraph 22. And now moving to paragraph 23 and your arrival at KP Dom Foca. Could you tell us what the people outside the prison who received you were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they say anything while beating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, they were cursing our balija mothers, insulted us in different ways, beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Radomir Matovic who you mentioned, did you see him again during the course of your detention at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him the whole time because he was the number one person in the kitchen, so he was preparing the food all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing during -- at the time you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: He was also wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the prison personnel who you name in your previous statement, Koroman, Mijovic, and Elcic, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Elcic -- yes, they were also wearing military camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the Serbs who travelled on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: They were locked up in one room, and then after two days they were sent to the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they also beaten when they arrived at the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I don't know that and I didn't have the opportunity to see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to move on in your statement to your time in which you describe as room 20 and room 11. That's -- the paragraph reference is number 23. Could you just tell us -- give us an idea of how many prisoners or how many detainees were present in room number 20?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: When I first arrived to the room, there were 21 of us. In less than a week, the room was filled with a total of 72 inmates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know largely where they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: All the inmates were from the area of the Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs among them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, once you were transferred to room number 11, do you have an approximate idea of how many detainees were held in that room?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know largely where they were from as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: They were all from the Foca area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any Serbs among them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No. There were just two Croats, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No, excuse me. There were three Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated in the corrections to your previous statement that during your detention in KP Dom you were beaten four times. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you locked in the solitary confinement cell after each beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, it always happened like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, in each case did the beatings take place in the solitary confinement cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: The beating was conducted in front of the solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the first and second occasions in paragraphs 26 and 27 of your 1995 statement, you say that two guards called you out and beat you and in fact you name one of the perpetrators. You identified one Zoran Matovic. Is this the same person who arrested you in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the third and fourth occasions you were beaten, do you recall who the perpetrators were on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Again, it was Zoran Matovic and Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you just give us an idea about the dimensions of the solitary confinement cells that you were held in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: 1 metre by 1 metre 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, with respect to paragraph 46 of your 1995 statement, you talked about cleaning the room in which the people had been beaten and mention that you saw blood in there. Did you see anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Wasn't it 45?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had the opportunity to clean that room. The walls and the floor were covered with blood and there were some wooden bats or the wooden handles of axes as well as some metal pipes strewn about the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to those 36 men who you saw called out, have you ever seen any of them alive again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No, I didn't -- haven't seen any of them. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have contacts with some of the families of the individuals who were called out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I had contacts with several families, and they told me that they themselves didn't know anything more than I did and that the bones of their close ones were never found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in some cases, have you in fact received information that the remains of some of these 36 have been recovered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes. Two were found. I know about those two, but I don't know anything about the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you this morning. Thank you, Witness 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we need a break anyhow, I'd like to take it now. We'll adjourn until quarter past 1.00. When the witness leaves the court, the curtains will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need a break of a little bit more due to the redactions which takes some time to be processed. Let's see whether 25 minutes will do. 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's one of the paragraphs that was not introduced, Your Honours, under 89(F), it was dealt with orally this morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- it was paragraph 9. You describe the radio broadcast that you had overheard of Mr. Ostojic. And then you said: "This was the only time I personally heard Ostojic ordering something. Lojo Taib who told me on several occasions that all orders were issued by Ostojic, Maksimovic, Cancar, Stanic, who were stationed at the Orthodox church in Cohodar at Mahala." When you gave evidence this morning, and this is at page 67 and it comes at line 3: "And do you recall what he told you?" And your answer was: "He told me directly all orders and the commands that were being issued in the town were under the auspices of Maksimovic and the Pale leadership and Ostojic." Now, when you gave your statement, Witness, that was 1995 and you made no mention in your detailed statement there of the Pale leadership. Do you think that perhaps that's something that wasn't staid but has come into your head over the last ten years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: As for the first question concerning Velibor Ostojic, I said that I had heard him for the first time issuing orders in wartime, and that was when I heard his voice over the radio station. As for the second question, from Taib Lojo, who was the president of the Municipal Assembly and who had met with the SDS leadership before and during the war, of course he knew where the obstacles that were placed in our way came from and where the orders came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, really what I'm putting to you is this: That three years after the events you gave an account in your statement where you just reported this other person as telling you that all orders were by Ostojic, Maksimovic, Cancar, and Stanic, and then 13 years after the event, here today in court, you introduce a reference to the Pale leadership. And I'm asking you whether perhaps that reference to the Pale leadership was not actually said in 1992 but is something that's just come into your head one way or the other over the last ten years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: In my previous statements, I was not asked to relate what I had just indicated here and it never occurred to me to do it myself, although I should have done it long ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I may put it very directly to the witness. Witness, Mr. Stewart would like to know why in 1995 when you said that other persons told you that all orders were issued by, and you mentioned a few people, a few names. And now you come with a larger description of who issued orders, that is the Pale leadership. Mr. Stewart would like to know whether this has not slipped into your mind one way or the other over the last ten years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I omitted that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is: Are you sure that they said at that time not the names you mentioned in 1995, but that they said that it was the Pale leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That person told me that it was mostly from the Pale leadership that the orders came from, or rather that the orders came up from -- up there from Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how did you then translate at that time the Pale leaderships and the names you mentioned, that is Ostojic, Maksimovic, Cancar, and Stanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maksimovic, Ostojic, Cancar were the local people who executed the orders, whilst at the same time Maksimovic and Ostojic were part of the Pale leadership and they were simply sent back to their town to do the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what they told you or is that what you, for whatever reason, conclude by now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what I was told and that is also a conclusion that I arrived at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago: "In my previous statements I was not asked to relate what I had just indicated here and it never occurred to me to do it myself, although I should have done it long ago." Are you saying that the suggestion about the reference to Pale leadership has come from somebody else rather than from yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No. Nobody suggested that to me, but probably I was bothered by the experience from the camp and I was preoccupied with my health and it only occurred to me now. I just hope it's not too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Krajisnik, do you have any questions for the witness? And I may remind you that protective measures are in place, Mr. Krajisnik. That also means that if the witness is answering the question, you should switch off your microphone. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I extend my greetings to the witness and I would like to put a question to him. Cross-examined by Mr. Krajisnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the witness says that he received information from the president of -- or rather, that the president of the municipality received orders from Pale, when did this take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: It took place right before the war. The president of the municipality was in contact with the president of the Executive Board of my municipality, Mr. Mladjenovic, and they together -- they were in contact together, they exchanged information, and knew what was going on in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that until after 8th of April the SDS leadership was in Sarajevo and not at Pale?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: As far as I know, the SDS leadership was active from Pale on the 8th of April because there was a war on in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber who the republican-level functionaries were from Foca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean? In terms of the party that they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean both in terms of the party and the republican level.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: During the war or?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the pre-war period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I was not that familiar with the leadership. I was not into politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to refresh your memory. Can you tell me who your deputies from Foca were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of Sahim Pasic and Cancar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you disagree with me if I told you they were the Foca deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina for both peoples?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I would not disagree because I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Muhamed Cengic from Foca also visited Foca, as did the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, Muhamed Cengic did come. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Velibor Ostojic, Muhamed Cengic, Vojislav Maksimovic, Sahim Pasic, Cancar -- were they all born in Foca or around Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, they were all born around Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Velibor Ostojic and Maksimovic lived in Sarajevo before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Maksimovic was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I used to see him at the meetings of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you clarify your answer. Was he a member of the SDS before the war and in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I would not be able to confirm that because I don't know. How should I know who the SDS members were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read quite a large article by Mr. Halid Cengic concerning the arming of the Muslims in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the beginning of the war there was no electricity in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, there was no electricity in Foca in the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who interrogated the inmates. Was it done by the civilian or military authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: The interrogators were from the military structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krnojelac competent or had he -- did he have competence over those who interrogated the inmates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your description of the solitary confinement cell, can you tell us whether the prison where you were kept had prior to the war been designated for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes. Even before the war KP Dom was a place where prisoners, offenders were held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the solitary confinement cell, was it used before the war for the purposes of the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 068
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. I thank the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Witness, 068 -- let me first see whether there are any questions. The Chamber has no questions for you. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this could not trigger any additional questions to the witness. Witness 068, I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and for answering the questions put to you. It was a short examination, but you are aware that the Chamber has available your written statements; they are in evidence as well. Perhaps it's practical that the witness waits for a second until this session is over so that we don't have to pull the curtains down at this very moment because of one or two short announcements to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, before those short announcements, could we deal with the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can deal with the exhibits. Relatively simple today. I take it we have P806 up to and including P810. They have all been described already. And I do not hear any objections, so therefore they are --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are admitted into evidence. And just to make sure, these are the redacted versions of the statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the protective measures they should all be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They should be under seal. Yes. I said that already for 806, but that's true for the others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must make one announcement in order not to lose pace, the Chamber is exploring whether we could have later this week some extended sessions. Primarily we are thinking about Thursday -- this is just to announce to the parties so that they are prepared and they could at this moment say that extended sessions would be impossible or would be preferred on Wednesday or Friday. There is some space in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just want to say straight away. I'm having a meeting with my co-counsel this afternoon, at which one of our major issues on the agenda is whether the present pace is manageable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A heavier pace, Your Honour, I can put that as item 1 be on our agenda this afternoon as well. But I will indicate, Your Honour, that to consider it may be, Your Honour, that in relation to (redacted) and well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not being difficult about it and I would think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. -- can we just turn to private session and could we have a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. Still with respect to the witness who is present before us, he doesn't speak anymore but face distortion should still be there if -- whenever he would be caught by one of the cameras. Yes, I do understand. I'm not talking about a dramatic -- it's rather regaining, although I understand that the same would be valid for regaining time lost. We're not talking about days and days, we're talking about to see whether we could finish with the witnesses scheduled for this week. But I took on board your observation, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
